sm: The episode opens with the day's headlines. President Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance honored veterans at Arlington National Cemetery, and Trump said he wants the Iran war to end only with total victory, while still hoping for a diplomatic solution. U.S. diplomats spent two days in Abu Dhabi with Ukrainian and Russian officials without a major breakthrough, though Jared Kushner said a large prisoner release was agreed. Democrat Scott Column won a Mississippi Senate seat by less than one percent, and Democrats and the White House traded warnings over planned House investigations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his family moved to a military base amid threats from Iran. The first feature begins on Republican efforts to make Trump's immigration orders permanent, with Freedom Caucus chair Andy Harris urging that border policies be locked into law.

Congressman Michael Cloud said loopholes in asylum law remain, while Maria Salazar promoted her Dignity Act, which offers legal status to long-term undocumented immigrants who pay fines. Nearly half of the Republicans who first backed it lost reelection, and Heritage Foundation analyst Simon Hankinson thinks little will happen in the lame-duck session. Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats prefer the Dream and Promise Act. Jenny Murray of the National Immigration Forum said moderates won and that many voters want a full solution for Dreamers. Trump said there will be no amnesty. The next story covered the new Education Freedom Tax Credit starting in 2027, which allows donations of up to 1,700 dollars a year to scholarship groups. Eighteen states have yet to opt in, and Vermont, New York, and Virginia are creating roadblocks, while an Oregon Democrat has proposed repeal.

Autumn Faulkner urged families to tell lawmakers how the credit could help them. Rachel Elgensmith of the Basic Fund said she expects public schools to benefit, and states must opt in by January 1st. Then Mary spoke with Jared Hayden of the Institute for Family Studies about AI in schools. His report found about four in ten schools allow or require AI, and most parents are more convinced of its harms than its benefits. Only 51 percent agreed that it prepares children for the future workforce. Utah and Tennessee are scaling back education technology. Hayden said nearly nine in ten schools have one-to-one devices, and that students excel on AI-assisted homework while test scores fall, because struggling with material helps retention.

A lighter story described German soccer fans in Bochum jumping in rhythm so that part of the stands bounced. Engineers said it was not unsafe, but the club banned synchronized jumping through 2028, when the stadium is renovated. The main feature was a conversation between World's Lindsey Mass and author Andy Noe about his book on the Zizians, a fringe group that began with obsessions about artificial intelligence and altruism and turned to violence. Noe said the group fits a larger pattern of violence by trans-identifying people. He accused media and law enforcement of obscuring suspects' sex and legal names, and said he insisted on using birth names. He said it took a lot of digging to learn the suspects' identities after the shooting of a Border Patrol agent.

Noe said the Zizians are not an isolated cult. He pointed to mental health comorbidities, autism diagnoses, cross-sex hormones and drugs, easy access to firearms, and an ideology of a ongoing transgenocide that fuels grievance. He said these factors create feedback loops and that more violence is likely. Next, Cal Thomas reflected on Benjamin Netanyahu's legacy after Israel's October 27 election. President Herzog asked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, and Netanyahu gets a turn only if he fails. Thomas called Netanyahu the best leader Israel has ever had, citing his rejection of land for peace, economic liberalization, and military and diplomatic strength. Tomorrow's show will include Culture Friday and a review of a new Christmas Carol film adaptation.
